sources.title: The Mughal Empire
sources.publisher: John F. Richards, Cambridge University Press, 1993

paragraphs.text: The Mughal Empire was founded by Babur after his victory over Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526. Its centre lay in northern India, with capitals and court residences including Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore, and Shahjahanabad at different times. At its greatest extent under Aurangzeb it claimed much of the subcontinent, but authority varied across provinces and decades. [0][1][2]

Mughal political life combined Timurid and Central Asian dynastic traditions with South Asian institutions, regional elites, and local systems. The dynasty formally ended after the 1857 uprising and the British government's subsequent transfer of power to the Crown in 1858; its effective empire had fragmented much earlier. [0][1]
The registry's 1526-1857 span marks the dynasty's conventional foundation and the deposition of Bahadur Shah II. It should not imply consistent imperial authority for all 331 years. [0][1]

paragraphs.text: Babur's memoir records the 1526 victory at Panipat and his 1527 victory at Khanwa over Rana Sanga's coalition. Humayun lost the throne to Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and restored Mughal rule in 1555, dying the following year. Akbar's long reign expanded the empire and strengthened court and revenue institutions. [0][2]

Jahangir and Shah Jahan maintained a powerful court and major building programmes. Aurangzeb's reign brought the empire to its greatest territorial extent but also prolonged Deccan wars and political resistance. Later emperors ruled with progressively less effective authority; Bahadur Shah II was deposed after 1857. [0][1]

paragraphs.text: Babur was a Timurid ruler from Ferghana who established a base at Kabul before entering northern India. Firearms, field artillery, cavalry tactics, and alliances contributed to his 1526 victory; the Baburnama is a first-person memoir but also a ruler's self-presentation. [0][2]

The dynasty's durable expansion followed Akbar's accession in 1556. He used conquest, marriage alliances, negotiation with Rajput rulers, and administrative integration; these policies varied by region and did not eliminate resistance. [0][3]

The First Battle of Panipat (1526) defeated Ibrahim Lodi; Khanwa (1527) checked Rana Sanga's coalition and strengthened Babur's position. Akbar's campaigns extended Mughal influence into Gujarat, Bengal, and other regions. [0][2]

At Haldighati in 1576, Mughal forces under Man Singh fought Maharana Pratap's Mewar army. Mughal forces held the battlefield, but Mewar resistance continued; describing the encounter as the definitive conquest of Mewar would overstate its outcome. Shah Jahan's sons later fought a succession war, with Aurangzeb defeating Dara Shikoh in 1658. [0][1]

Aurangzeb's Deccan campaigns against the sultanates and Marathas expanded Mughal claims but required long, costly occupation. Regional resistance, succession conflicts, and continued warfare weakened the imperial centre without producing one single collapse event. [0][1]

Akbar's mansabdari system ranked imperial officers by zat status and sawar cavalry obligation; jagir assignments connected many officials' remuneration to land revenue. The system changed over time and relied on negotiation with local elites. [0][3]

Todar Mal's zabt assessment used measured land, crop rates, and average prices over a ten-year period in some core regions. It was not applied uniformly across all provinces. The empire was divided into subahs governed by provincial officials; Abu'l-Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari is a contemporary compendium with courtly and administrative purposes. [3]

Agricultural land revenue formed the fiscal base of the empire. Textile production, crafts, metalwork, and urban markets supported internal exchange, while Indian Ocean trade connected ports with West Asia, Africa, and Southeast Asia. [0][1]

Silver rupees, gold mohur, and copper dam circulated in changing monetary contexts. Revenue systems and commercial conditions differed by region; court records do not prove that all subjects shared equally in imperial wealth. [0][3]

The empire governed populations speaking many languages and following diverse religions. Persian court chronicles describe elites and administration; regional records, European travel accounts, and local archives reveal other perspectives. [0][1]

Women exercised documented roles as rulers, patrons, authors, and members of the imperial household, including Nur Jahan and Jahanara Begum. These exceptional court examples should not be taken as a complete account of women's lives across the empire. [0]

Mughal religious policy varied by ruler. Akbar sponsored debates and the principle of sulh-i kul, or peace with all; Jahangir, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb made different choices in law, patronage, and political practice. [0][3]

Hindu, Muslim, Jain, Sikh, and other communities interacted through courts, towns, and regional institutions. A single description of Mughal religious policy across three centuries would obscure these changes and local variation. [0][1]

Mughal architecture includes Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, the Red Fort, gardens, and the Taj Mahal. The Taj was commissioned under Shah Jahan and is listed by UNESCO as a major Mughal monument. [4]

Court painting and illustrated manuscripts developed through imperial workshops and regional exchange. Persian, Chagatai, and South Asian languages appear in court and literary cultures; patronage changed across reigns. [0][1]

The Mughal court supported astronomy, medicine, cartography, engineering, and manuscript production through particular scholars and workshops. The Ain-i-Akbari documents measurement and administration; it should not be treated as a catalogue of every scientific practice. [3]
Military artillery, waterworks, gardens, and monumental construction demonstrate applied technology. Knowledge circulated among Indian, Persianate, Central Asian, and European practitioners. [0][1]

Mughal territory expanded from northern India toward Gujarat, Bengal, the northwest, and the Deccan at different times. The displayed map depicts an early eighteenth-century reconstruction; it should not be read as the extent of the empire in every reign. [0][1]
Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore, and Shahjahanabad served as important capitals or court centres at different moments. Provincial authority and princely relations varied across this broad space. [0]

Succession wars, expanding regional states, fiscal and military pressure, and repeated invasions weakened the imperial centre after Aurangzeb. Nadir Shah's 1739 sack of Delhi exposed this vulnerability; Company power expanded in the eighteenth century. [0][1]

Bahadur Shah II was deposed after the 1857 uprising. The British Crown formally abolished Mughal sovereignty in 1858; this formal end is distinct from the much earlier loss of effective imperial power. [0][1]

Mughal administrative forms, Persianate literary culture, painting, gardens, and architecture shaped later South Asian states and cultural histories. The empire also remains central to debates about regional politics, religious policy, and colonial transitions. [0][1]
The Baburnama and Ain-i-Akbari are primary sources with distinct authorial and court purposes. John F. Richards provides a scholarly synthesis; UNESCO documents the Taj Mahal specifically.

The Maratha polity began as a seventeenth-century kingdom under Shivaji and became a major eighteenth-century confederacy. The registry uses 1674-1818, from Shivaji's coronation to the end of Peshwa independence; the confederacy's regional houses continued as princely states under British paramountcy. [0][1]

Power was shared among the Chhatrapati, Peshwa, and important houses such as the Holkars, Scindias, Gaekwads, and Bhonsles. The structure changed over time and was not a continuously centralized empire. [0]
Maratha dates distinguish the founding kingdom, Peshwa-led expansion, confederacy, and later defeat by the Company. [0][1]

paragraphs.text: Shivaji built a kingdom based on forts, mobile warfare, diplomacy, and revenue administration and was crowned at Raigad in 1674. Sambhaji resisted Mughal expansion; Rajaram and Tarabai continued the war from southern strongholds. Shahu's return in 1707 reshaped relations between the royal house and Peshwas. [0][1]
Peshwas including Baji Rao I and Balaji Baji Rao expanded Maratha power, while Holkar, Scindia, Gaekwad, and Bhonsle houses developed considerable regional autonomy. [0]

Shivaji rose amid the Deccan sultanates and Mughal expansion, building a regional following in the western Deccan. His coronation asserted sovereign kingship; the later empire grew through military campaigns, negotiated tribute, and Peshwa-led alliances. [0][1]

After Aurangzeb's death, Mughal central authority weakened and Maratha commanders expanded north. This process produced a confederacy whose constituent houses pursued both shared and competing interests. [0]

Shivaji's forces used hill forts, mobile cavalry, local intelligence, and coastal vessels in conflicts with the Mughals and Deccan powers. The First and Second Anglo-Maratha Wars ended in treaties but did not end Maratha sovereignty. [0]

At the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761, Ahmad Shah Durrani's coalition defeated the Marathas. The losses were severe, but Maratha power recovered in the following decades; the battle was not the end of the confederacy. [0][2]
The three Anglo-Maratha wars ended with the Third War of 1817-1818, after which the Peshwa surrendered and the Company expanded paramountcy over the remaining houses. [0]

Shivaji's administration included the Ashta Pradhan council, fort commanders, revenue officers, and local authorities. The council is a court model associated with his reign, not proof that every successor used an unchanged centralized system. [0][1]

Revenue claims such as chauth and sardeshmukhi supported expansion, while Peshwas coordinated diplomatic and military networks. Confederacy houses administered their own territories and negotiated with the Peshwa and Chhatrapati. [0]

Agriculture and land revenue formed the fiscal base. Chauth and sardeshmukhi were claims on revenue in territories beyond the Maratha core and should not be treated as a uniform tax paid everywhere. [0][1]

Western ports, inland routes, crafts, and customs connected Maratha centres with Indian Ocean commerce. Shivaji developed coastal defenses and naval forces, though maritime capacity varied across later rulers. [0]

Maratha politics drew on landed elites, military households, administrators, merchants, and cultivators across varied regions. Court and colonial records emphasize political elites and provide uneven accounts of everyday life. [0]

Women such as Tarabai exercised documented political and military leadership during the succession crisis after Rajaram's death. Her case is important but should not be generalized to all women's status. [0]

The Chhatrapati court patronised Hindu institutions, while the Maratha state employed and negotiated with people of different religions. State policy varied by ruler and circumstance; it should not be reduced to a single religious description. [0][1]
Bhakti traditions and local temple networks shaped regional society, but religious practice differed across the confederacy's wide territories. [0]

Hill forts such as Raigad, Pratapgad, and Sinhagad shaped Maratha defense and political geography. Court centres at Satara and Pune and the later confederate capitals reflected changing administration. [0]
Maratha architecture included forts, temples, palaces, and urban institutions. Their construction histories are local; the accompanying map shows territorial power rather than a monument. [0]

Fortification, mobile cavalry logistics, coastal defense, and revenue record-keeping were important practical systems. Shivaji's naval development is documented, but no single empire-wide scientific academy is established by the sources. [0][1]
Knowledge of terrain, supply lines, and monsoon-season movement supported military campaigns; specific engineering claims should be tied to individual forts or records. [0]

Maratha influence expanded from the western Deccan across central and northern India in the eighteenth century. The map depicts a proposed extent around 1760; the confederacy's houses held distinct territories and influence varied over time. [0][1]
The Third Battle of Panipat took place far north of the Maratha homeland, showing the reach and logistical demands of Peshwa-era campaigns. [2]

The defeat at Panipat in 1761 weakened but did not end Maratha power. Later rivalries among confederate houses and the three Anglo-Maratha wars steadily reduced independence; the Peshwa surrendered in 1818. [0][2]
Several Maratha princely states continued under British paramountcy. Their survival does not extend the sovereign confederacy beyond the registry's 1818 endpoint. [0]

Maratha history is central to the transformation of Mughal-era politics and the rise of Company power. Forts, revenue practices, regional houses, and military networks shaped later western and central Indian states. [0][1]

Stewart Gordon's study is a specialist history of the Marathas from 1600 to 1818. Panipat and the Anglo-Maratha wars are described through multiple Persian, Maratha, and British accounts with differing perspectives.

sources.title: The Sikhs of the Punjab
sources.publisher: J. S. Grewal, Cambridge University Press, 1990

paragraphs.text: The Sikh Empire was a Punjab-based state established by Ranjit Singh, who captured Lahore in 1799 and was crowned Maharaja in 1801. It expanded across Punjab and adjoining northwest regions and lasted until the East India Company annexed Punjab in 1849. This state is one chapter in the wider history of Sikh communities, not a synonym for Sikh history. [0][1]
Lahore was the capital. The empire governed a religiously diverse population and employed Sikh, Hindu, Muslim, and European officers at different times. [0]
The empire's formation followed the Sikh misls; its end came after two Anglo-Sikh wars and a period of post-Ranjit Singh court instability. [0][1]

rows: Founded the Sikh Empire conventionally dated 1799-1849.

Succession and court factions destabilized the state.
Company victory and treaty reduced Sikh autonomy.
Ended with annexation of Punjab by the Company.

paragraphs.text: Ranjit Singh unified competing Sikh misls and built a court at Lahore. After his death in 1839, Kharak Singh, Nau Nihal Singh, Sher Singh, and Duleep Singh succeeded amid factional struggles and changing control by the Khalsa army and court nobles. [0][1]
Duleep Singh was a child when he became Maharaja; regents and military leaders exercised power. The sequence culminated in British annexation in 1849, after which the boy was deposed and exiled. [0]

After the decline of Mughal authority in Punjab, Sikh misls formed confederated political and military communities. Ranjit Singh consolidated several misls and captured Lahore in 1799, then used diplomacy and military action to build a centralized kingdom. [0][1]
The empire developed alongside Afghan, cis-Sutlej, and Company powers. The 1809 Treaty of Amritsar limited expansion east of the Sutlej and shaped relations with the British. [0]

Ranjit Singh expanded through campaigns in Punjab, Kashmir, Multan, and the northwest. The army was reorganized into infantry, cavalry, and artillery units with European-trained officers, while the Khalsa army remained a central political institution. [0][1]

The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845-1846) ended in Company victory and territorial concessions. The Second War (1848-1849) followed uprisings and military escalation, ending in the annexation of Punjab. [2][3]

Ranjit Singh's government used a royal court, provincial governors, military commanders, and revenue officials. Administrators came from Sikh, Hindu, Muslim, and other backgrounds; authority and practice varied among regions. [0][1]

Lahore was the principal capital, with regional centres including Amritsar, Multan, and Peshawar. Revenue collection supported the court and army, but records do not establish a uniform system across all conquered territories. [0]

Agriculture in the Punjab plains supported state revenue. Trade routes connected Lahore with Central Asia, Kashmir, and northern India; the empire's expansion brought commercial centres and borderlands under its influence. [0][1]
Customs, land revenue, and local levies supported military modernization. The evidence is not a complete account of tax rates or the distribution of prosperity. [0]
The empire ruled Sikh, Muslim, Hindu, and other communities. Ranjit Singh's court employed officials from different backgrounds, while provincial experience and representation varied. [0][1]
Court chronicles and later colonial accounts focus on elites and conflict. They provide less direct evidence for women's daily roles and rural custom across Punjab. [0]

Sikh institutions held a central place in the kingdom. Ranjit Singh patronised Sikh shrines and also donated to Hindu and Muslim religious sites; these documented acts show court patronage, not uniform experience among all subjects. [0][1]
The empire should be distinguished from the wider history of Sikh communities, which predates and continues beyond the 1799-1849 state. [0]

Ranjit Singh's patronage at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar included gilding associated with its present appearance. Lahore's forts, gardens, and court collections reflect the empire's cosmopolitan material culture. [0][1]
The displayed flag is a modern historical reconstruction credited to its creator; it is not itself a contemporaneous state document. [1]

The army adopted European-style infantry drill and artillery alongside regional military practice. Fortifications, gun foundries, and logistics supported expansion; the modernization was associated with particular officers and periods, not a single uniform transformation. [0][1]

The empire centred on Lahore and at its height extended across much of Punjab toward Kashmir, Peshawar, and the northwest frontier. Borders changed with campaigns and treaties; the map is not a fixed survey. [0][1]
The Treaty of Amritsar in 1809 defined a limit of Company and Sikh influence near the Sutlej; later wars and annexation transformed the frontier. [0]

After Ranjit Singh's death in 1839, succession disputes, court assassinations, and conflicts between the Khalsa army and the Lahore court weakened central authority. The First and Second Anglo-Sikh Wars ended in the Company's annexation of Punjab in 1849. [0][2][3]
Duleep Singh was deposed and exiled. Punjab became part of British India, while Sikh political, religious, and community histories continued beyond the empire. [0]

The Sikh Empire was the last major independent kingdom in Punjab before British annexation. Its military institutions, diplomacy, and plural court are central to nineteenth-century regional history, while Sikh identity and history extend far beyond the state. [0][1]

J. S. Grewal's study provides scholarly context for Sikh and Punjab history. The Anglo-Sikh War pages summarize campaigns; treaty records and court documents offer primary evidence for specific events.

sources.publisher: Barbara D. Metcalf and Thomas R. Metcalf, Cambridge University Press

paragraphs.text: This entry covers two distinct political regimes: East India Company rule and British Crown rule. Company power expanded through commercial privilege, war, diplomacy, and revenue administration from the mid-eighteenth century; Crown government followed the 1857 uprising and was established by the 1858 Act. British rule ended with independence and Partition in 1947. [0][1][2][3][4]

1757 marks the Company's victory at Plassey and an important stage in its political expansion, not uniform British control over the whole subcontinent. Company authority remained regionally uneven and coexisted with princely states until Crown rule and beyond. [0][1]

The registry's 1757-1947 span is an umbrella chronology. Company political power expanded after Plassey (1757) and the diwani grant (1765); Crown rule began in 1858 and ended in 1947. These are not dates for uniform control of the entire subcontinent. [0][1][2][3][4]

Government of India Act and Jallianwala Bagh
Reform expanded limited representation; massacre intensified opposition.

Congress launched mass resistance during the Second World War.

paragraphs.text: The Company was governed by directors and presidencies, then by governor-generals; it was a corporation and not a hereditary dynasty. Under the Raj, the British monarch was sovereign and the viceroy headed imperial government, while princely rulers retained internal authority under paramountcy. [0][1][2]

On the Indian side, Siraj ud-Daulah, Mir Qasim, Tipu Sultan, Rani Lakshmibai, Bahadur Shah Zafar, and many other rulers and leaders held distinct roles in regional resistance. Gandhi led Congress mass campaigns; Nehru was a Congress leader and later the first prime minister; Bose organized the Indian National Army and Azad Hind government; Patel led post-independence integration of princely states; Ambedkar led anti-caste political work and chaired the Constitution's Drafting Committee. These roles were different and should not be conflated. [0][1][5]

paragraphs.text: The East India Company arrived as a trading corporation under a 1600 charter. Its political power expanded in Bengal after Plassey in 1757, where Siraj ud-Daulah was defeated amid elite defections and Company intervention. This was a regional turning point, not the beginning of uniform rule across India. [0][1]

At Buxar in 1764, Company forces defeated the combined armies of Mir Qasim, Shuja ud-Daula, and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. In 1765 Shah Alam granted the Company diwani revenue rights in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa; this formalized an important fiscal power while sovereignty remained layered. [0][1]

Company expansion involved the Anglo-Mysore, Anglo-Maratha, and Anglo-Sikh wars, as well as campaigns against other states. Outcomes depended on regional alliances, military technology, and revenue; the Company did not conquer the entire subcontinent in one campaign. [0][1]

The 1857 rebellion included sepoy mutinies and civilian and princely uprisings in parts of north and central India. Causes included military grievances, annexation, revenue and land policies, and fears about religious and social change; participation and aims differed by region. It was not a uniform movement involving every Indian community. [0][1]
The rebellion was suppressed by Company forces with support from some Indian rulers and communities. It led Parliament to end Company government and establish Crown rule in 1858. [3]

Company government developed presidencies, courts, revenue departments, and an expanding civil and military service. Parliament regulated the Company through successive acts; administrative practice differed between directly governed territories and princely states. [0][1]

The Government of India Act 1858 transferred authority from the Company to the Crown. The Raj retained provincial administrations and princely states under paramountcy, with constitutional reforms changing the council and franchise system over time. [3]

Company revenue rights and trade policies redirected economic flows toward imperial priorities. Land settlements such as Permanent Settlement, ryotwari, and mahalwari differed regionally; their effects on cultivators, landlords, and revenue extraction varied. [0][1]

Railways, ports, and telegraphs expanded under Crown rule, supporting administration, troop movement, and commerce. Historians debate the balance between infrastructure's later uses and its original imperial purposes; industrial change and deindustrialization also varied by sector and region. [0]

Colonial censuses, legal categories, education, and administration reshaped public institutions, while their effects varied by community and locality. Famines under Company and Crown rule were linked to crop failures, market conditions, policy, and relief decisions; causes and responsibility are subjects of historical debate. [0][1]

Education, urban professions, migration, and new political organizations changed social life. Women participated in reform, education, and political movements, but colonial sources and elite narratives document their lives unevenly. [0]

Religious reform movements included the Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Prarthana Samaj, and Aligarh movement, among others. They arose from Indian intellectual traditions and colonial institutions and differed in theology, education, and social reform; they were not simple one-way Western influence. [0]

Anti-caste movements and leaders including B. R. Ambedkar challenged social hierarchy and shaped constitutional debates. Their political work was distinct from, and sometimes in tension with, Congress strategies. [0]

Colonial-era architecture combined European, Indo-Islamic, and regional forms in railway stations, courts, museums, and government buildings. Indian artists, writers, and printers also developed new forms in response to changing markets and institutions. [0]
Print, vernacular journalism, novels, and political pamphlets expanded public debate. These cultural changes varied across languages and regions. [0]

Railways, telegraphs, canals, surveys, universities, and modern medical institutions expanded under colonial administration. They served imperial extraction and governance, while Indian engineers, workers, and institutions adapted and later used them for new purposes. [0]

The development of infrastructure and scientific institutions had uneven access and effects. Specific technical achievements should be tied to documented institutions and people rather than attributed to colonial rule as a single actor. [0]

British power expanded unevenly from coastal trading bases through Bengal and other regions. By the Raj, British India included directly administered provinces and princely states under indirect rule; the 1909 map depicts one imperial administrative moment, not the Company's territorial reach in 1757. [0][2]

Partition in 1947 divided British India into India and Pakistan. Boundary-making, migration, and later state formation changed the political geography and affected communities across Punjab, Bengal, and other regions. [4][6]

Anti-colonial politics developed through Congress, Swadeshi after the 1905 Bengal partition, revolutionary organizations, labor and peasant movements, and regional groups. Gandhi led Non-Cooperation (1920-22), the Salt March and Civil Disobedience (1930 onward), and Quit India (1942). Bose organized the Indian National Army; these movements had different strategies and constituencies. [0][5]

The 1946 Cabinet Mission negotiations and conflict over power-sharing preceded the 1947 transfer. Partition divided Punjab and Bengal and created India and Pakistan; millions were displaced, communities experienced mass violence, and death toll estimates remain contested. Princely states faced separate accession decisions. [0][4][6]

Colonial rule left administrative, legal, economic, linguistic, and infrastructural institutions, alongside extraction, famine, dispossession, and lasting political consequences. Historical interpretation remains contested and benefits from Indian and regional perspectives as well as imperial records. [0]

Independence and Partition created sovereign states and new borders in 1947. The political, human, and geographical consequences remain part of the histories of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. [4][6]

The Government of India Act 1858 and Indian Independence Act 1947 are primary legal sources. Metcalf and Metcalf provide a scholarly synthesis; Company and Crown periods must be distinguished, and the 1857 revolt is treated as regionally varied.
